doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: College, the Red Onions, first gigs, Tip Toe Inn and the union
summary: Clarinet heroes, a fraternity improvising test, a Bridgeport gig and getting his union card amid anecdotes of union corruption.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I liked Sidney, yeah. I liked Sidney a lot and then not later on I fell in love with Omer Simeon, the clarinet player with Jelly Roll Morton and he played with Wilbur DeParis you know on 52nd Street. So now I get into college, and even then I’m improvising and playing little gigs and stuff and I joined the Phi Mu Alpha Symphonia, you know, a fraternity, and part of the test initiation was you had to improvise, you had to play at a jam session. And everybody was terrible, well they were all classical musicians you know. And we had this thing and I’m wailing away, and they’re looking, “what the hell? Where’d you get that?” You know it was completely unexpected. I was going to become a music teacher. So where were we? So that’s how I started to play. And I think after, with the crowd I was with that was with Irv Kraken who was a trumpet player. There was a guy named Jerry Bloomberg. Jerry was a wonderful player. He was sort of like, he loved Bunk Johnson, and he could play like Bunk very much, you know, he was quite a good player. He maybe — and you know who maybe was on it? The guy, the short guy that played trombone some with Louis’ big band. He played with Clarence Williams in the 20s. I can’t think of his name. He was on it too. So I did that, and that was my first gig as I said that paid some money. And then I was scratching around. There used to be a joint in Bridgeport, Connecticut called the Tip Toe Inn. And they paid some sort of $20 and drinks or whatever, which didn’t interest me much. I didn’t smoke or anything, you know. And the pot was around, but I was not interested in that. It was years later that I smoked a joint you know. Oh no. So you know, getting into the musical world such as it was, so we played this gig in Bridgeport and it was always trouble. There was a union guy would come around and see — I think he was really interested in the tax you know, which is really all he ever wanted, to see your card you know. So it was a big — I think I joined the union, I joined the union when it was on I think 54th and Sixth. And I went up and they put up music, I read it and I got my card. I mean there were other guys who went up there and they couldn’t play at all. Bob Green, the piano player, told me there
was a piano player and they put music in front of him and he played some Jelly Roll Morton thing. And they said, “you’re not reading the music.” He said, “well this is my interpretation.” He got in.
Yeah. The audition wasn’t that official.

Yeah. It showed the corruption of the union in those days. And that building on the corner there, 54th or 52nd and Sixth, wherever it was, they could have bought for something like $50,000, which would be worth a billion dollars today you know. They could have had a permanent home and they didn’t buy it they just kept renting it. Probably somebody got a kickback you know.
